newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany faces rise of "environmental militants".
newsitem.headline: Germany faces rise of "environmental militants".

text.p: Germany's anti-nuclear activists, who on Friday protested against controversial atomic waste shipments, have become a thorn in the side of the authorities who have to mount increasingly costly operation to combat them.
While protests have been mainly peaceful, activists in the green lobby are increasingly turning to illegal means to press demands for a nuclear-free world, German law enforcement officials say.
Militants have resorted to railway sabotage -- often with grappling hooks thrown onto overhead lines -- and bomb threats, the officials say.
"Those who encourage non-violent resistance (in anti-nuclear protests), know that in all likelihood they are abetting violence," Interior Minister Manfred Kanther told parliament this week.

When nuclear waste shipments started arriving in 1995 at the Gorleben medium-term storage depot -- the chief focus of anti-nuclear protests -- the normally-peaceful northern German farmland looked like it had been hit by civil war.

Again last May, thousands of protesters staged sit-down protests on the tracks, farmers blocked roads with tractors and others sought to damage the rails in a massive effort to stop the 40-tonne shipment of French-processed atomic waste.

In a vast security operation, about 19,000 police, riot police and border guards with helicopters were deployed all along the train's route but mainly in Lower Saxony, where the Gorleben site is located, to ensure its safe arrival.
They succeeded, but at a price.
It was one of Germany's most costly operations and triggered a still-unsolved row between cash-strapped regional authorities and Bonn over who should pay for future operations.
A German court ordered 14 anti-nuclear activists this month to pay damages for holding up work at Gorleben in 1990, saying their political opposition did not justify breaking the law.
But such cases seem set to increase protesters' resolve rather than deter future resistance.

"We are investigating several such cases at present who we believe are not just isolated individuals but operating as part of an organised group of militants," Frauke Scheuten, a spokeswoman for the Federal Prosecutor's Office, told Reuters.

"There are various groups behind many of these attacks. Some are militant anti-nuclear activists, while others are members of the left-wing scene who have latched on to that movement to express their opposition to the state," Scheuten said.

German ecology groups reacted with horror earlier this month after a train carrying nuclear waste derailed in France, saying it proved what they had always said -- that nuclear shipments were potentially lethal and should be stopped.

The opposition Social Democrats and the Greens party led the outcry, but Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government defended its record saying that in the last 20 years some 1,500 nuclear waste shipments had left Germany to be processed in Britain or France without any serious incidents.
